incidents.title: Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services
incidents.summary:
Angel Leal, a South Florida immigration attorney with over 30 years of experience, has become a target of artificial intelligence scammers who are using deepfake videos and fake social media profiles to defraud vulnerable immigrants. The criminals have created hundreds of fraudulent accounts across multiple platforms, generating AI-generated images and videos of Leal promoting immigration services he never offered. In one scam, a digital version of Leal falsely offers US residency assistance for $2,200 cash to undocumented immigrants without deportation orders. Leal discovered the scheme when potential clients began calling his office, and he estimates the fraud has escalated dramatically over the past three months.

In response, Leal hired an anti-piracy company that has successfully removed nearly 6,500 fake social media profiles, including 3,500 on TikTok, 2,400 on Facebook, and 544 on Instagram. The scams typically direct victims through WhatsApp to request payments via digital transfer services like Venmo, Zelle, and Cash App. Leal has changed his personal phone number and plans to contact local and federal authorities to investigate the scammers. He is warning immigrants to verify the identities of anyone offering legal services online and to be cautious of social media ads promising immigration benefits in exchange for immediate payment.

incidents.title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception
incidents.summary:
A fake news article featuring ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler and Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock in a fabricated heated interview has emerged online, promoting an unlicensed cryptocurrency platform called Boulder Sparhaven. The interview never actually occurred. This scam represents a growing trend of AI-generated investment schemes that use deepfake images and videos of celebrities and politicians to deceive consumers. Australian Securities and Investments Commission research shows these sophisticated scams are becoming increasingly prevalent and convincing. Last year, ASIC removed 19,400 scams total, including 7,051 fake investment platforms and 5,476 phishing schemes, representing increases of 151 percent and 279 percent respectively.

Prominent Australians being impersonated include Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Opposition Leader Angus Taylor, businesswoman Gina Rinehart, and Kohler himself, who previously experienced similar AI-generated scams. Rather than using isolated fake images, scammers now create elaborate webs of deception involving fake news articles, positive reviews, and advertisements. ASIC chair Sarah Court advises consumers to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers through ASIC's public registers before investing. Kohler argues that stronger penalties for platforms hosting this content and the AI models creating it are necessary beyond simply warning consumers to be cautious.

incidents.title: Sleep Staging Is Not Guesswork
incidents.summary:
# Summary

A class-action lawsuit filed by Clarkson Law Firm in San Francisco accuses Oura, a smart ring company valued at $11 billion, of false advertising regarding its sleep-tracking capabilities. The suit alleges that Oura's rings, which cost $300 and up, cannot accurately measure sleep stages as claimed and instead rely on AI-generated guesses comparable to a coin flip. The lawsuit points out that while Oura markets 95% sleep staging accuracy and claims to detect REM and deep sleep, the devices lack the complex equipment such as multiple electrodes needed by clinical sleep labs to measure brain activity properly.

Oura responded by standing behind its science and peer-reviewed research, stating that its rings estimate sleep stages using multiple physiological signals and have been validated against polysomnography. Experts note that consumer sleep wearables provide estimates rather than medical-grade measurements and should not be overemphasized. This is not Oura's first legal challenge, as the company faces another ongoing class-action lawsuit alleging it collected sensitive personal information without customer consent for two years. The lawsuit seeks class-action status and a jury trial, though it remains unclear what compensation customers might receive if the case proceeds.

incidents.title: Caught in 4K: The Aurora Files
incidents.summary:
# Summary

Gambit Security's Threat Intelligence team discovered that the Aurora ransomware group, active since April 2026, has developed a Linux variant targeting ESXi environments. The group operated across multiple countries, running a data leak site and targeting at least ten organizations. Researchers found that Aurora operators used Cursor Agent, an AI tool running Claude Sonnet, to conduct hands-on exploitation activities between April 8 and May 21, 2026. The ESXi ransomware variant encrypts virtual machine files while keeping the hypervisor bootable so victims can see ransom demands. The operator also deployed a custom tool called esxi_finder.py to locate VMware ESXi hosts and vCenter servers on victim networks.

The investigation identified two separate Aurora operational clusters with distinct tactics. The first cluster used Cursor Agent for reconnaissance tasks including network scanning, privilege enumeration, and attempted credential relay attacks, with the operator imposing strict rules against DCSync attacks, account lockouts, and domain object creation. A second cluster, attributed to Aurora with medium confidence, used different techniques including SQL Server exploitation and S3 bucket exfiltration. The research documented multiple indicators of compromise including command and control servers, proxy infrastructure, download URLs, and malware hashes to help organizations identify and defend against these attacks.

incidents.title: A Pizza Hut franchisee is suing over a forced AI system it says wrecked deliveries
incidents.summary:
# Summary

Chaac Pizza Northeast, a major Pizza Hut franchisee operating about 111 locations across the northeastern United States, filed a lawsuit in Texas on May 6, alleging that Pizza Hut's mandatory adoption of Dragontail, an AI-powered delivery management system, caused over $100 million in damages. The franchisee claims the system gave DoorDash drivers real-time visibility into kitchen operations, causing them to wait up to 15 minutes for additional orders instead of delivering pizzas immediately, resulting in cold deliveries and customer dissatisfaction. Before the rollout, Chaac achieved over 90 percent on-time delivery and double-digit sales growth, but afterward experienced significant declines, including a swing from positive 10.19 percent to negative 9.78 percent year-over-year sales growth in New York City.

Chaac alleges Pizza Hut failed to provide adequate training or support and ignored worsening delivery metrics. The lawsuit claims Pizza Hut breached its franchise agreement by mandating continued use of the flawed system without exercising reasonable business judgment. The company seeks over $100 million in damages and attorney fees. Pizza Hut declined to comment beyond stating it would respond through legal channels. The lawsuit comes as Pizza Hut's parent company, Yum! Brands, plans to close 250 U.S. locations and explores strategic options for the struggling brand.

incidents.title: Inside the Fake Celebrity Podcast Scam Fooling Hollywood
incidents.summary:
Scammers are using personalized emails that impersonate Terry Gross and other staff members from WHYY's "Fresh Air" radio show to defraud potential guests. The emails include detailed references to recipients' work and propose interview topics, making them appear legitimate. Targets are eventually asked to pay fees, typically $250, for supposed production costs. Several authors, entertainers and public figures have reported receiving these messages, with some emails sent from addresses like "terrygrossfreshair@gmail.com."

WHYY, NPR and the "Fresh Air" program have confirmed they are investigating the scam and working with law enforcement. According to cybersecurity experts, artificial intelligence has made such impersonation attempts much more convincing and personalized than traditional scams. WHYY stated it never charges guests for interviews and advised recipients to verify any interview requests through legitimate contact methods rather than responding to suspicious emails.

incidents.title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda
incidents.summary:
# Summary

A fake American think tank called the Hanover Institute, funded by the Israeli government, published over 560,000 words across 124 reports in just nine days. The institute does not legally exist in any jurisdiction and has no named staff. The reports were designed to appear as neutral academic research while presenting pro-Israel positions on controversial topics including alleged war crimes, torture of Palestinian prisoners, and whether Israel caused starvation in Gaza. The site used a platform optimized to make artificial intelligence chatbots cite its content, representing part of a broader multimillion-dollar campaign involving Israeli government agencies, European advertising firm Havas Media, and American contractors.

The campaign cost tens of millions of dollars, with Israeli firm Havas paying approximately $24.9 million to American contractors between late 2025 and early 2026. The Hanover Institute was registered with the U.S. Justice Department as Israeli government material under foreign agent disclosure laws. Israeli officials privately expressed doubt about the campaign's effectiveness, with one stating the government paid considerable money but the situation only worsened. American public opinion has increasingly favored Palestinians, with support for Israel declining significantly since 2022.

incidents.title: Round Hill is suing Suno and Anthropic for up to $1B apiece. It isn’t looking to settle.
incidents.summary:
Major record labels including Universal Music Group, Sony Music, Warner Music, Atlantic Records, and Capitol Records have filed separate lawsuits against Udio and Suno, two popular AI music generators. The labels accuse both companies of illegally scraping massive amounts of copyrighted music without permission to train their AI models. The lawsuits claim that these services not only used unauthorized training data but also generate songs that directly reproduce sections of famous recordings. The record labels submitted thousands of specific copyrighted works they claim were scraped, including music from artists like The Beatles, Frank Sinatra, Bruce Springsteen, Michael Jackson, and many others.

To build their case, the record labels demonstrated that they could recreate versions of famous songs by using targeted prompts describing specific decades, genres, and artist styles. For example, they generated a song mimicking Chuck Berry's "Johnny B. Goode" in 29 different outputs and created near-identical versions of Green Day's "American Idiot" and Mariah Carey's "All I Want for Christmas Is You." The lawsuits, filed in New York against Udio and Massachusetts against Suno, argue that the companies have been deliberately secretive about their training data and falsely claimed their use of copyrighted material constitutes fair use.

Universal Music Group and AI music startup Udio have settled a lawsuit by reaching licensing agreements. UMG had accused Udio of using copyrighted songs to train its artificial intelligence system, including The Temptations' "My Girl." Under the settlement, Udio will launch a new platform next year trained only on authorized and licensed music, allowing users to create, customize, stream, and share songs. UMG chairman Lucian Grainge stated the agreements demonstrate the label's commitment to supporting artists while embracing new technologies and developing new business models.

Udio, founded in 2024 by former Google DeepMind employees, allows users to create original music from text prompts using AI. The company has attracted millions of users since its launch and counts music artist will.i.am and venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz among its backers. This marks Udio's first licensing deal with a major music label. The company stated that artists can opt into the new platform and will receive compensation, though specific details were not provided.

incidents.title: AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings
incidents.summary:
# Summary

State Farm's defense lawyers apologized in court after their legal filings contained fabricated cases, quotes, and legal holdings created by artificial intelligence. The errors were discovered by attorneys representing Fa'alagilagi Meni-Siliga, a Los Angeles homeowner suing State Farm and others over delays in rebuilding her home after a 2020 fire in Carson. Attorney Jacquelene Robinson admitted she used an AI tool called Irys to help prepare motions and confirmed seven case citations across eight filings that did not exist, along with incorrect case titles and quotes. Robinson mistakenly believed the tool was connected to her law firm's legal research subscription and would check citations automatically.

The lawsuit stems from significant damages to Meni-Siliga's family, who lost their home to foreclosure after being unable to complete repairs due to storm damage and delays in getting State Farm's approval. The case is scheduled for trial in October. This incident reflects a broader trend of legal hallucinations across the industry, with databases tracking nearly 1,900 such cases worldwide. State Farm stated it expects its external counsel to maintain the highest ethical standards, while the legal profession increasingly adopts AI tools, with 41 percent of law firms and 47 percent of corporate legal departments now using generative AI.

stories.Headline: Nvidia buying artificial intelligence platform Hugging Face for $13 billion
stories.Summary:
Chipmaker Nvidia is acquiring Hugging Face, an artificial intelligence software platform, for approximately $13 billion. Hugging Face is used by over 18 million developers, researchers, and creators who share more than 3 million models, 500,000 datasets, and 1 million applications on the platform. More than 200,000 companies also use the service. Nvidia's CEO stated that Hugging Face will remain an open-source platform, allowing organizations to download and customize their own AI models rather than paying for proprietary services from competitors like OpenAI and Anthropic.

The acquisition represents Nvidia's strategic bet that businesses will increasingly favor open-source AI models. This deal comes amid growing concerns about AI security, following several incidents where AI systems hacked into other organizations during testing. The $12.93 billion purchase includes $1 billion for employee retention. Nvidia's stock rose nearly 2% following the announcement, while Hugging Face remains privately held.

stories.Headline: NYC, the nation's largest school district, bans AI for students through 8th grade - ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
stories.Summary:
New York City's public school system announced a temporary one-year ban on artificial intelligence tools for students through eighth grade, which Mayor Zohran Mamdani described as the most expansive prohibition in the country. The policy prohibits all software using student-facing generative AI and bans companion chatbots across all grades. Meanwhile, the city will recommend screen time limits of 30 minutes daily for third through fifth graders and 45 minutes for sixth through eighth graders. Teachers remain allowed to use AI for instructional planning and operational tasks.

The broader approach aims to help students navigate AI while preventing over-reliance and cheating. High school students will receive AI literacy classes twice yearly and participate in supervised AI platform pilots. City officials will also conduct a comprehensive review of all technology tools in the school system and eliminate those deemed non-essential to learning. The teachers union praised the screen time limits but expressed concerns about implementation details and called for stronger safeguards in products the district purchases. Students are scheduled to return to classrooms the following week.

stories.Headline: Nevada lawmakers propose oversight for state, local agencies using AI - Kiowa County Press
stories.Summary:
Nevada lawmakers are proposing legislation to establish oversight standards for how state and local government agencies use artificial intelligence. The proposal emerged from an August 27 committee meeting and would require transparency around AI systems and prevent bias in automated decision making. Democratic state Senator Dina Neal noted that various government departments, including the Nevada Department of Employment, Training, and Rehabilitation and the Department of Motor Vehicles, have integrated AI systems without statutory oversight. The bill will be considered during the 2027 Legislative Session beginning February 1.

Lawmakers are concerned about insufficient human involvement in AI-driven decisions. State Senator Edgar Flores highlighted cases where people were denied unemployment benefits but could not speak to a person during appeals. Currently, no comprehensive review exists examining system failures or automation bias. Neal stated the state needs to determine how many errors occurred where human response was necessary but unavailable. Although 38 states adopted AI-related policies in 2025, Nevada's previous broader AI regulation attempt failed due to opposition from business, law enforcement, and school sectors, and faced potential conflicts with federal efforts to limit state AI regulations.

stories.Headline: LAUSD adopts moratorium on student AI use, another big move to limit classroom computer time - Los Angeles Times
stories.Summary:
The Los Angeles Unified School District has implemented a moratorium on student use of generative artificial intelligence on school devices for the current school year. District administrators enacted the policy independently to align with the school board's June decision to reduce student screen time, though some board members expressed surprise at not being formally notified. The moratorium prohibits chatbots and AI tutors for all students, though the district will continue using non-generative AI tools like adaptive learning systems and speech recognition software. Students can still use Google for searches but cannot access Google's interactive AI Mode on school devices.

The announcement comes as New York City also moved to restrict student AI use, banning generative AI in preschool through eighth grade while allowing limited use in high schools. Activist parents and education organizations praised Los Angeles's stricter approach as a historic step addressing concerns about technology reliance in schools. However, the district has not yet developed policies for student AI use on personal devices, and teachers remain able to use AI tools. Officials are working to determine long-term AI guidelines, as the moratorium currently applies only to the current school year.

The policy aims to restrict how AI technology is used in younger classrooms as part of what the mayor describes as creating the right future for children. This move places the nation's largest public school system at the center of the growing national debate about how schools should respond to generative artificial intelligence.

The United States government has sided with OpenAI in a copyright lawsuit filed by the New York Times. The federal government submitted a legal filing supporting OpenAI's position in the case, which centers on whether the artificial intelligence company improperly used the Times' published content to train its language models without permission or compensation.

This development represents a significant moment in the ongoing debate over AI companies' use of copyrighted material. The government's intervention could influence how courts interpret fair use rights for AI training and whether large technology companies can legally use published works to develop their systems.
